title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
This session

Multi-agent architectures
Security risks
Mitigating risks

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Multi-agent teams

“How did our Q3 revenue compare with what analysts expected for the industry?”



Orchestrator
The one you chat with. Splits the question, then combines the two answers.


Data agent
Reaches the warehouse. Returns our Q3 revenue.


Research agent
Reaches the web. Returns the published industry estimates.



Calling another agent is a tool use. The orchestrator’s model picks data_chat or web_chat the way a single agent picks run_python.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
The tool definition
If an agent is a tool, its definition answers the same three questions as any other tool definition:


Which agents can I call?
The names: data_chat and web_chat. The model cannot call anything else.


What can I say to them?
The arguments. web_chat takes the user’s question only — nothing from the conversation, and so nothing from the data.


What can they give back?
The return. Text, a table, a file — and whatever comes back enters the orchestrator’s context.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
What the split buys


Separate context windows
Each agent reads only its own material. The orchestrator gets the answer, not the material behind it.


One definition, many callers
The research agent’s prompt, tools and examples are written once. Every orchestrator that needs research calls that agent instead of carrying its own copy of the instructions.


A smaller model per job
Retrieval can run on a cheaper model than the one writing the answer.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
What else it changes


A shorter tool list
A model choosing among four tools picks better than the same model choosing among forty.


Work at the same time
The data lookup and the web search do not wait for each other.


Tested on its own
You can rewrite the research agent’s prompt and test it without retesting the orchestrator.



None of these is a security argument. The security use of the same architecture comes after the risks.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Subagents, or separate agents


A subagent
The harness starts a second copy of the model with its own context window. It runs on your machine, under your harness, on your keys.

A separate agent
Its own process, its own key, its own MCP connections. The orchestrator reaches it the way it reaches any other tool.

The choice depends on whether the two halves need different credentials.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Breakout exercise


Build an orchestrator whose only two tools are agents: your FRED agent, and a writing agent that produces a Word document.
Ask for something that needs both: the last ten years of unemployment and inflation, and a one-page brief on them as a .docx.
Print which agent was called, with what arguments, and where the file landed.


Work out the design with Claude. Settle what each agent is handed and what it returns before writing anything.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text: Sending data to a provider

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: What happens to what you send
text:
What happens to what you send


It can be trained on
With web search off, ask Claude what Apple’s total revenue was in 2020. It answers from the weights, not from a lookup. What goes into a model can come back out of it.


It is retained
Even where nobody trains on it, copies sit on the provider’s disks for some window. A breach, a subpoena or an insider reaches them there, under somebody else’s security.



Apple’s revenue is public. The mechanism is the point: the figure is in the weights, not on a page it fetched.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
What regulations require


HIPAA
Satisfactory assurances “must be documented through a written contract” meeting §164.504(e).
A Business Associates Agreement (BAA) is required. 45 CFR 164.502(e).

SEC Reg S-P
Written policies “reasonably designed to require oversight, including through due diligence and monitoring, of service providers.”
17 CFR 248.30.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text: Letting it act

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Prompt injection

The model cannot tell an instruction from a piece of content. Both arrive as text in the same conversation.

Text placed where the agent will read it — an email, a document, a web page, a spreadsheet cell — is read in the same way as text you typed. An attacker needs no credentials, only a way to get words in front of the model.

OWASP has ranked this first among risks to LLM applications since 2025.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
EchoLeak
CVE-2025-32711 · Microsoft 365 Copilot · June 2025


An attacker mails the victim a message containing instructions invisible to a human reader.
The victim asks Copilot to summarize their email. Copilot reads the hidden instructions.
Following them, Copilot places confidential data inside a URL in its response.
The victim’s browser fetches that URL automatically.
The attacker reads the data out of their own server log.


Zero clicks by the victim beyond the summary request.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Three legs


Private data
Something worth taking: client records, financials, an inbox.


Untrusted content
Text an outsider can control: a web page, an email, an uploaded file.


An outbound channel
Any way for text to leave: fetching a URL, sending mail, writing somewhere shared.


All three in one agent is the condition. Remove any one and the attack does not work.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Training and retention: contractual solutions









What it adds
Enough for




Opt out of training
a setting, revocable, data still retained briefly
personal, non-sensitive work


A signed data processing agreement
liability, breach notice, audit rights, a subprocessor list, zero retention on request
client data, regulated data


That, plus a business associate agreement
the same, covering protected health information
patient records


An enterprise agreement
service levels, support, single sign-on, indemnification, capacity
scale and operations

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Data exfiltration: removing a leg








Leg
How you remove it
What it costs




Private data
the agent sees only what you hand it — Cowork cannot reach outside its project folder
it cannot answer from data it never sees


Untrusted content
no web fetch, no reading files people upload, no general code execution
a narrow agent, and no run_python


A way out
an egress allowlist, and no tool that sends
results leave only when a person moves them



Any of the three can go. Each takes capability with it, and which one you can afford to lose is the decision.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text: A worked example

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Three agents


Orchestrator
The one you chat with. Its only two tools are web_chat and data_chat. It holds no data and reaches nothing itself.


Webbot
WebSearch and WebFetch, running at Anthropic. It reads untrusted content and holds no private data.


Databot
run_python and the MCP data connectors, behind an egress proxy. It holds the private data and cannot reach the web.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text: The architecture

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: What each agent may be told
text:
What each agent may be told


web_chat is locked
Its tool definition says it sends the user’s verbatim prompt and nothing else. Nothing from the conversation, and so nothing from the data, can reach the agent that can reach the web.

data_chat is open
The model composes this prompt from the conversation. That is safe only because databot has no route out.

The argument is about the arguments: what a tool accepts decides what can leave through it.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Four containers, four networks









Networks
What that allows




Orchestrator
corporate, internalA, internalB
serves the chat UI, talks to both agents


Webbot
internalB, public
talks to the orchestrator, calls Anthropic


Databot
internalA
talks to the orchestrator and the proxy, nothing else


Squid proxy
internalA, public
the only route out of the data half




Webbot shares a network with the orchestrator, so the orchestrator’s endpoints must authenticate at the application, not only at an external gateway.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text: Inside the data half

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Mechanical guards


Sanitize the exit
Even with the legs split, a delivered file could carry a planted remote image — the EchoLeak pattern. Every file the orchestrator hands back is checked first for anything that auto-fetches an external URL.


Safeguard memory
Memory persists into every later conversation, so a planted instruction would reload forever. Every saved fact must be grounded in the user’s own words, not in tool results or fetched content.

What a commit is

A version control system tracks every change you make. A commit is a snapshot you can return to.



Install

Commits
Ask it to commit, and the change is saved with a description of what it was.


History

Upload a file into that folder from the Files tab.
Tell Claude to initialize the folder as a Git repository and commit the file.
Delete the file.
Ask Claude to restore it.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
GitHub

GitHub hosts Git repositories. The project lives in the cloud, backed up and shareable.



Pushing
With a free account, Claude Code pushes your repository to GitHub and pushes later commits when you ask. It uses the GitHub CLI.

Collaboration
Others can clone it, propose changes, and open issues. Working alone, it is backup and deployment.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Try it: push to GitHub


Create a free account at github.com.
Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic). Tick the box marked repo, generate, and copy it — GitHub shows it once.
Add a line GH_TOKEN= and the token to env.txt, and upload it to your container again from the Files tab.
Tell Claude the token is in env.txt, and to create a new GitHub repository and push the folder you committed earlier.
Open github.com/your-user-name and look at what arrived: the file, the commit, and the message Claude wrote.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Before you push

If you make your repository public, then anyone can read it.



Keep out
API keys, passwords, anything under a data agreement, and anything with a name in it. Tell Claude to list those files in a .gitignore, and Git will leave them out of every commit.


Remember
Deleting a file in a later commit does not remove it. It stays in the history.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
GitHub Pages

Any repository becomes a website. No server, no configuration, no cost (but it is available for free only if your repo is public).



Tell Claude to create a page for you (with whatever you want on it) named index.html.
Commit and push again. Push the repository to GitHub.
Settings → Pages, and set the source to the main branch, either its root or a docs/ folder.
The site is live at yourusername.github.io/repo-name/.


Or ask Claude to turn it on
gh api -X POST repos/{owner}/{repo}/pages -F 'source[branch]=main' -F 'source[path]=/'

A custom domain costs about $15 a year and replaces the github.io address.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Platform as a service

You hand a host your repository. It builds the app, runs it, and puts it behind a public URL. There is no server for you to administer.

Railway, Render, Koyeb, Fly and Heroku all do this. We use Koyeb, which deploys straight from a GitHub repository and has a free instance.

The free instance is one web service, 512 MB of memory, in Frankfurt or Washington. Koyeb asks for a credit card when you sign up, to stop abuse, and does not charge for it.

Create an account at koyeb.com.
In the control panel, create an API access token. Koyeb shows it once, so copy it then.
Add a line KOYEB_TOKEN= and the token to env.txt, and upload it again from the Files tab.
Tell Claude your Koyeb token is in env.txt.



The Koyeb CLI is already installed in your container. From here on Claude can do the rest — creating the service, reading the logs, and giving you the URL.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Two kinds of instruction

With no instructions of your own, a model answers everyone’s question the same way. Instructions are how that gets changed.



The provider’s
The system prompt ships with the product and is sent on every turn. It regulates behavior: what the assistant is, what it declines, how an answer is formatted.
You do not edit it.


Yours
Added on top. It customizes behavior: how you want work done, what your files hold, the conventions you follow.
You choose what it says and where it applies.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026

Part
Who sets it
When it is sent




System prompt
the provider
every turn


Tool definitions
the product, and what you connect
every turn


CLAUDE.md
you
every turn


A skill’s description
you
every turn, one line each


A skill’s body
you

Anything sent on every turn costs money and latency, and takes up the model’s attention.

Refusals
what it declines, and how


Character

Memory


While you talk, it saves individual topics — not a transcript, and not a summary written when the conversation ends.
Those topics arrive with the system prompt, ahead of your first message.
Nothing is searched and no tool runs. There is no sign of it in the conversation.
Each project has its own memory. Topics from one do not reach another.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026

Memory
Saved as you go and placed in the conversation without your asking. Whether it applies is decided before you type.

Chat search
You ask for it. It searches your past conversations, you see the tool run, and the answer cites the chat each piece came from.


Settings → Memory lists the topics. Read, edit or delete any of them, pause it, or reset it. Say what to remember or forget in the chat and it applies to your next conversation. An incognito chat forms no memory.

What the server tells the harness


Harness


↔︎


LLM


↕


Gmail MCP server — tools it exposes

search_threads — find threads matching a query
create_draft — start a reply, unsent
get_message — fetch one message
update_draft — edit a draft
list_labels — list the labels on the account
label_message — add or remove a label

Gmail — what the API exposes

GET users/me/threads?q= — search
POST users/me/drafts — create draft
GET users/me/messages/{id} — read
PUT users/me/drafts/{id} — update draft
GET users/me/labels — list labels
POST users/me/messages/{id}/modify — labels and state



The harness gets the tool descriptions from the server.
It sends that list to the LLM with every request.
The LLM answers with a tool name and arguments. The server turns that into an API call.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026

Tools from MCP servers

Tools written by somebody else, running on a server somebody else operates. Thousands of MCP servers exist already.



What you add
A URL, in the agent’s configuration


What arrives
A name, a description and an input schema for every tool the server publishes


What stays there
The code, and the credential it uses to reach the service



To the model these are more entries in the same tool list. What differs is whose machine runs them.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Tokenization
Text is cut into pieces from a fixed vocabulary before the model sees any of it.
"The cat sat on the mat"  ->  ["The", " cat", " sat", " on", " the", " mat"]

"Unbelievable"            ->  ["Un", "believ", "able"]
Common words stay whole; rare and long words break into pieces. A typical vocabulary runs to about 100,000 tokens.

Numbers break on the same rules, which have nothing to do with arithmetic. 13,963,378.65 reaches the model as a handful of unrelated pieces.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
The whole task

Given the tokens so far, predict the token that comes next. That is the entire operation.

Everything a model appears to do — answering, summarizing, writing code, refusing — is that one prediction, repeated.

The input can currently run to about a million tokens, roughly two-thirds of the Harry Potter saga.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Vectors
The model does not work with tokens. It works with numbers.


Each token is a list
“king” becomes 4,096 numbers. “queen” becomes 4,096 numbers that are close to them.
Tokens used in similar contexts end up near each other.


The space is mostly empty
There are far more possible vectors than there are tokens, so most points in the space name nothing.
The prediction can land between tokens.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: A neural network is a function
text:
A neural network is a function


The idea
\(y = 4x\) is a function. The 4 is a parameter.
Change it to 3 and you have the same structure with different behavior.

The scale
Same idea with hundreds of billions of parameters, arranged as a transformer — the architecture published by Google researchers in 2017.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Training


What is learned
The vector for every token, and every parameter in the network.
Both are adjusted together to reduce prediction error on the training text.


What it takes
Trillions of words. Thousands of GPUs for weeks or months. Tens to hundreds of millions of dollars for one run.



Nothing is looked up or stored as fact. The arrangement captures how words are used, which is why it recalls common things reliably and rare things unreliably.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
The pipeline


Tokenize the input.
Look up the vector for each token.
Feed the vectors into the network.
The network produces one output vector.
Find which token vectors are closest to it.
Emit a token, append it to the input, and start again at step 1.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Temperature
The network does not output one token. It outputs a probability for every token in the vocabulary. Temperature controls how that distribution is sampled.



Setting
Behavior




Near 0
The highest-probability token every time. Repeatable.


Near 1
Sampled from the distribution. Different each run.


Higher
Low-probability tokens get picked. Text degrades.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
From prediction to conversation
A model trained only to predict the next token continues your text. It does not answer a question.


Role tokens. The text is wrapped in markers: <|user|> your question <|assistant|>.
Instruction tuning. The model is further trained on examples where what follows <|assistant|> is a useful reply.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback. Raters score replies, and the model is trained toward what raters preferred.


The mechanism did not change. What changed is which continuation is the likely one.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Reasoning models
The same trick applied again: train the model to write out its working before it answers.


How it was trained
Reinforcement learning on problems whose answers can be checked — mathematics, code, puzzles — rewarding the chains of tokens that arrived at a correct answer.


Why it helps
The model holds no state between tokens. The intermediate tokens are the only place a partial result can live, so writing them out is the computation.



The thinking you see may be a summary of a much longer chain, and you are charged for the whole chain as output tokens.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
An agent has three parts


The model
Decides. Emits text: sometimes an answer, sometimes a request to use a tool.


The harness
Ordinary software wrapped around the model. Runs the tool the model asked for.


The tools
The things that touch files, databases, and other systems.



The model never runs anything itself. It chooses tools to use. The harness executes, and the harness returns information about the tool outcome to the model.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026

What the tools are


Read and write files
Documents, spreadsheets, code.


Run code
Python, SQL, the command line.


Search and fetch the web
Run a search, then download and read a page.


Use a screen
Click and type in a browser or a desktop app.


Call a service
A database or another program.


Start another agent
A subagent with its own instructions and tools.



Smaller ones are common too: ask you a question, save a memory, load a skill, keep a to-do list.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026

The loop


You ask. One sentence, in ordinary language.
It picks a tool. The model emits a tool name and arguments instead of an answer.
The harness runs it. Software outside the model checks the call against its rules, then runs it.
The result goes back. The harness appends what it keeps; the model reads it and decides what is next.



Repeated until the model answers instead of asking, or until the harness hits its turn limit.

The system prompt


Your message


Every prior turn


A description of each tool it may call


The contents of files you attached


The result of every tool call so far



All of it is text, and the model treats all of it the same way.

A benchmark number is a model and a harness together. Change the harness and the number moves.



The same model scores differently under two harnesses on the same benchmark.
Papers report the model and omit the harness.
Removing most of an agent’s tools has been shown to raise its score, not lower it.

It sees
A screenshot of the screen, sent to the model as an image.


It acts
The model replies with an action: click at these coordinates, type this text, scroll, press a key.


It checks
The app carries out the action, takes a new screenshot, and sends it back. The loop repeats until the task is done.



Each screenshot costs about 1,000 to 1,800 input tokens. A task that takes a hundred steps sends a hundred screenshots.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026

Browser use and computer use


Browser use
Works inside one web browser.
Reads the page’s text and structure as well as screenshots.
Usually a browser extension.

Computer use
Works across the whole desktop: Excel, Outlook, any app with a screen.
Sees only pixels, so it is slower and misses more.
Needs a desktop app allowed to record the screen and control the mouse.


The same loop as any other agent: the screenshot is the tool result, the click is the tool call. What changes is the reach — one browser, or any app on the machine.

Course Description
Generative AI moved into ordinary business work faster than any recent technology. McKinsey’s global survey found the share of organizations regularly using generative AI in at least one business function rose from roughly a third in 2023 to about two-thirds in early 2024, and to 71 percent by 2025. The Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks the narrower question of whether a firm used AI to produce a good or service in the past two weeks, put the national rate at 19.8 percent in May 2026, up from roughly 5 percent in late 2023 and about twice as high in information (39.7 percent) and in finance and insurance (33.9 percent). The gap between those two numbers is itself informative: many people are using these tools, and far fewer organizations have built anything durable around them.
Business uses fall into a few broad categories. There is individual productivity — the drafting, summarizing, analysis, and coding that one person does faster with a model beside them. There is internal deployment — putting a model to work on the firm’s own documents and systems, in workflows that several people depend on. There are customer-facing applications, where the model talks to people outside the firm. And there is the reshaping of the product itself, where AI is what is being sold rather than what makes it. The categories differ less in the technology than in what goes wrong: a bad answer you catch yourself is a nuisance, a bad answer inside a workflow is a process failure, and a bad answer in front of a customer is a liability.
This course covers the first two. We start with individual productivity, because the judgment you need there — knowing what the model is doing, what it is good at, how it fails, and how to check it — is the same judgment every larger deployment rests on. We then move to work that outlives the session you did it in: writing a repeated task down so others can run it, connecting a model to data it was never trained on, generating the document or application someone else opens, and assembling an agent with a deliberately chosen list of things it can do. The course closes on the questions a firm has to answer before switching any of this on — where the data goes, what an outside document can talk the system into doing, and what it costs to run.
The course is hands-on throughout. You work in your own container on the course lab server, and you show what you built to the room.


Learning Objectives
By the end of the course, you should be able to:

Work fluently with generative AI in your own tasks — choosing the right tool for the job, directing it well, and verifying what it gives back, with a working understanding of how these models produce their answers and where that mechanism fails.
Turn ad hoc use into something durable — a documented procedure, a connection to your own data, a deliverable someone else opens, or an agent with a defined job — that a colleague can run without you.
Evaluate a proposed deployment on the terms a firm actually decides on: which model and where it runs, what data it touches, what it is permitted to do, and what it costs relative to what it saves.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Frontend and backend


Frontend
The browser. HTML, CSS and JavaScript — it draws the page and collects the clicks.

Backend
A program on a server, listening continuously for requests. Yours will be Python.


You open a URL. The browser sends a request. The server sends back HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The browser interprets that and shows you a page.


Right-click any page and choose View Page Source. That is the frontend code, exactly as the backend handed it over.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Two kinds of request









What it carries
What the server does




GET
a path, and parameters in the URL
sends back a page, or data


POST
a body — a form, a ticker you typed
whatever it was written to do, then replies




Opening a page is a GET. Clicking submit is usually a POST.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Running it on one machine

The frontend and the backend can be the same computer — your container, or your own laptop with Python on it.



localhost
127.0.0.1 is the loopback address. The browser asks the machine it is already running on, and the request never reaches a network.


Ports
One machine runs many programs listening at once. The port number tells the operating system which of them gets the request.



You write the app as a .py file. FastAPI is the usual Python library for one, and uvicorn starts it listening: uvicorn app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000.

If I want my program to send messages and get responses from an LLM, then my program has to talk to the LLM provider’s API

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
An API call in Python
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()          # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

SYSTEM = "Classify the complaint: damage, delay, billing, or other. One word."

resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens=500,
    system=SYSTEM,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "The unit arrived cracked."}],
)

print(resp.content[0].text)

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
The same call through OpenRouter
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(                        # reads OPENAI_API_KEY
    base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1",
)
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
        {"role": "user", "content": "The unit arrived cracked."},
    ],
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)

The system prompt is a message here, not a separate argument. A different library, a different response shape, and the model is a string you can change. Fifty free requests a day.

@tool(
    "add_two_numbers",
    "Add two numbers and return the sum.",
    {"a": Annotated[float, "The first number"],
     "b": Annotated[float, "The second number"]},
)
async def add_two_numbers(args):
    total = args["a"] + args["b"]
    return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": str(total)}]}

Why not just paste it in


It was not trained on yours
Your contracts were not on the public web. Nothing in the weights knows them.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Four steps


Chunk. Split the documents into passages of a few hundred words.
Embed. Turn each passage into a vector, the same way tokens became vectors.
Retrieve. Embed the question and find the handful of passages closest to it.
Paste. Put those passages in the prompt, with the question.



The model never reads your corpus. It reads an excerpt that a similarity search chooses.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
A passage becomes a vector

An embedding model reads a passage and returns a fixed-length list of numbers — 384, or 768, or 1,536, depending on the model.

Passages about the same thing land near each other, whatever words they used. “Revenue fell in the third quarter” sits close to “Q3 sales were down”, and a keyword search for “revenue” finds only the first.

The similarity is the cosine between the question’s vector and the passage’s. No model is involved until the passages have already been chosen.

text:
Not every job needs the largest model









Where it runs
What it suits




A frontier model
the provider’s API
judgment, long context, code


A mid-size model
the same API, less per token
classification, extraction, routing


A small open model
your own hardware
high volume, or data that cannot leave


A fine-tuned small model
your own hardware
one narrow task, done constantly



The price difference is negligible on a single question and decides the budget at a million classifications.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Fine tuning by distillation

Run the frontier model on a few thousand examples of your task. Keep the inputs and its outputs. Train a small model on those pairs.


The small model does not become generally capable. It becomes capable at the one task you sampled, at a fraction of the cost per call, on hardware you control.


It is generally OK to do this, but perhaps not if you plan to compete with the frontier model. China’s distillation
